Grammar That Changes Meaning

The grammar points where a mistake is not just an error but a different message.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • ✓Use past, present, and future to place events in time clearly
  • ✓Use articles where their absence changes meaning
  • ✓Form questions that get the answer you want
  • ✓Use modal verbs to ask rather than demand
📘 Reading Lesson

Lesson Notes

Read through the key concepts before you try the challenge.

Some errors are noise; these ones change the message

On the job

You are explaining an absence to a supervisor.

You say "I work yesterday." Your supervisor understands you. Later you say "I can work Saturday" when you meant "I could work Saturday" — and now they have you on the schedule.

Your task: Focus on the grammar that changes what people do, not the grammar that only sounds wrong.

Many grammar errors are harmless: a listener understands and moves on. A smaller set genuinely changes the message, and those are worth your attention first. Tense places events in time, modals signal how firm you are being, and articles sometimes change which thing you mean.

The last two rows are the ones that cause real trouble at work. "I will work Saturday" is a commitment. "I could work Saturday" or "I would work Saturday if you need me" is an offer. Supervisors act on the first, so use it only when you mean it.
Worked example

Turning a demand into a request

You need a coworker to swap a shift with you.

  1. 1

    Avoid the bare imperative: not "Swap shifts with me Thursday."

    In English an imperative to a peer sounds like an order. Many languages use a direct form politely; English marks politeness with modals instead, so the direct form reads as rudeness even when none is meant.

  2. 2

    Use "could" and add the reason: "Could you swap Thursday with me? I have a class that evening."

    "Could" makes it a request rather than an instruction, and the reason gives them something to say yes to. English speakers expect a short reason with a request between peers.

  3. 3

    Give them a way to say no: "If it doesn't work, no problem — I'll ask Marcus."

    This removes the pressure and makes a yes genuine. It also protects the relationship, which matters more than this one shift.

Result: A request they can accept or decline without awkwardness.

🔑 Could + reason + an easy way out. That is the standard shape of an English workplace request.

Check your understanding

Your supervisor asks if you are available Saturday. You are willing but would prefer not to. What should you say?

Challenge

Apply what you've learned in this lesson.

Focus on the forms that change meaning.

  1. Write six sentences about your own work using each tense in the table once.
  2. Rewrite these as polite requests: "Give me the schedule." "Tell me when you finish." "Change my shift."
  3. Write one sentence committing to something and one offering it, and mark the difference.
  4. Listen for "could you" and "would you mind" over one day and note who says them and when.
